passage: My English teacher keeps writing 'be more critical' on my essays. Fine. My next essay on the assigned novel trashes it from the first page to the last: boring plot, flat characters, terrible ending. Being critical is literally what she asked for, so this one better get an A.
cue: Being critical is literally what she asked for
explanation: Jaylen's teacher means 'critical' as in careful analysis; Jaylen takes it as 'negative.' A one-sided takedown isn't what she asked for just because the same word covers both.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Jaylen isn't distorting an argument to attack it; he's sliding between two meanings of the word 'critical.'

passage:
Customer: I'm on your Unlimited plan, but after 25GB my speed dropped so low I can't even load a map.
Agent: I understand. But the plan is unlimited: you can keep using data all month and we never cut you off.
Agent: So you're getting exactly what Unlimited promises.
cue: the plan is unlimited: you can keep using data all month and we never cut you off
explanation: The customer reads 'unlimited' as full-speed data with no cap; the agent switches to 'never fully cut off.' The conclusion only works because the word changes meaning mid-argument.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: The agent isn't misrepresenting the customer's complaint so much as quietly redefining 'unlimited' to make the plan look honest.

title: Re: Should we run the Delmar story?
passage: Thanks for flagging the concerns, Pia. I agree the restaurant-review angle is weak and the photos need work. But the teaser about Chef Delmar's divorce got 40,000 clicks in an hour. When the public is this interested, running it is in the public interest. Let's publish at noon.
cue: When the public is this interested, running it is in the public interest.
explanation: Grant slides from 'the public is interested' (people are curious) to 'the public interest' (what benefits the community). Lots of clicks show curiosity, not that the story serves the public.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: The clicks aren't offered as proof the story is true or good because it's popular; the trick is the shift from 'interested' to 'the public interest.'

title: Beat the 3 p.m. slump
passage: Feeling drained by mid-afternoon? Each can of Kickwell Fizz delivers 210 calories of pure energy, more energy than four cups of black coffee combined. Lightly sparkling, real citrus flavor, no artificial colors. When you need energy to finish the day strong, why settle for less?
cue: 210 calories of pure energy, more energy than four cups of black coffee combined
explanation: Kickwell uses 'energy' in the calorie sense, then sells it as the feeling of being alert. Coffee has almost no calories but plenty of caffeine; more calories doesn't mean more pep.

whyNot.fal_false_analogy: The ad isn't comparing two unlike things on shared features; it's swapping the calorie meaning of 'energy' for the alertness meaning.

title: Superintendent cites 'significant' sleep study in phone ban push
passage: In a randomized trial at two high schools, students asked to put phones away at 9 p.m. slept an average of four minutes longer. Researchers called this statistically significant: strong evidence of a difference, even a small one. Superintendent Rhonda Kaplan said late-night phones have a significant effect on students' health, large enough to justify a district-wide ban.
cue: late-night phones have a significant effect on students' health, large enough to justify a district-wide ban
explanation: The study uses 'statistically significant' for evidence of a difference, even a small one. Kaplan treats it as meaning large or important, but the measured difference is just four minutes of sleep.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: The trial was randomized, so cause isn't the weak spot; the slip is reading 'statistically significant' as 'large.'

passage:
Corinne: The Halcyon invoice went out two weeks late. Finance says their billing system was down.
Mark: Lena's responsible for the Halcyon account, right?
Corinne: Yes, since March.
Mark: Then she's responsible for the late invoice. I'll note it in her review.
cue: Then she's responsible for the late invoice.
explanation: Mark moves from 'responsible' meaning in charge of the account to 'responsible' meaning at fault. Lena can own the account without being to blame for Finance's system outage.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Mark isn't distorting anyone's argument; his conclusion rests on the word 'responsible' changing meaning between lines.

title: Re: Is the new onboarding flow worth it?
passage: Short answer: the improvement is small. The test result was statistically significant, meaning strong evidence of a difference, even a small one. 'Significant' in that sense doesn't mean large, though: completion rose from 71% to 72.5%. Given the $80,000 rebuild cost, I don't think the gain justifies a full rollout yet.
cue: 'Significant' in that sense doesn't mean large, though
explanation: Dr. Renn spots the two meanings of 'significant' and keeps them apart: evidence of a difference versus a large difference. His conclusion rests on the size of the effect, not on the word.

whyNot.fal_equivocation: Instead of sliding between meanings, Dr. Renn names both senses of 'significant' and reasons from the right one.

passage:
Ngozi: The site says free shipping on orders over $35. My cart was $38, but with the coupon it's $31.
Alex: Doesn't the $38 count as the order?
Ngozi: I checked the terms: they define the order total as the amount after discounts. So I'm under the threshold and won't get free shipping.
cue: they define the order total as the amount after discounts
explanation: 'Order total' could mean before or after the coupon, but Ngozi looks up how the store defines it and sticks to that meaning. Her conclusion follows.

whyNot.fal_equivocation: Ngozi settles the ambiguous phrase with the store's own definition and uses it consistently, so no meaning shifts mid-argument.
